claim: The eye's optics are a major determinant of visual perception.
source: The eye's optics are a major determinant of visual perception.
evidence: This is a foundational statement in the abstract that draws from established scientific consensus about visual processing.

claim: Keratoconus patients showed altered contrast sensitivity under fully-corrected optical conditions, with impaired sensitivity for fine spatial details and better-than-typical sensitivity for coarse spatial details.
source: Under fully-corrected optical conditions, keratoconus patients showed altered contrast sensitivity, with impaired sensitivity for fine spatial details and better-than-typical sensitivity for coarse spatial details.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract, supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: Both gains and losses in sensitivity were more pronounced in patients experiencing poorer optical quality in their daily life.
source: Both gains and losses in sensitivity were more pronounced in patients experiencing poorer optical quality in their daily life and mediated by changes in signal enhancement mechanisms.
evidence: This finding is stated in the abstract and supported by correlation analyses presented in the results.

claim: Changes in contrast sensitivity in keratoconus patients are mediated by changes in signal enhancement mechanisms.
source: Both gains and losses in sensitivity were more pronounced in patients experiencing poorer optical quality in their daily life and mediated by changes in signal enhancement mechanisms.
evidence: This mechanistic finding is stated in the abstract and supported by perceptual template model analysis in experiment 3.

claim: Adult neural processing adapts to better match the changes in sensory inputs caused by long-term exposure to altered optics.
source: These findings show that adult neural processing adapts to better match the changes in sensory inputs caused by long-term exposure to altered optics.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract, inferred from the pattern of experimental results.

claim: Human optics are not fixed and can substantially change over our lifespan and in disease.
source: Human optics, however, are not fixed and can substantially change over our lifespan and in disease (Artal, 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Visual processing adapts to the presence of optical blur, altering neural processing to improve visual representations.
source: There is growing evidence that visual processing adapts to the presence of optical blur, altering neural processing to improve visual representations (e.g., Artal et al., 2004; Sawides et al., 2011; Webster, 2015; Webster et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Neural adaptation mechanisms compensate for blur-induced reductions in physical contrast of high spatial frequency retinal signals, enhancing visual sensitivity for fine spatial details.
source: Neural adaptation mechanisms compensate for blur-induced reductions in physical contrast of high spatial frequency (SF) retinal signals, enhancing visual sensitivity for fine spatial details (George and Rosenfield, 2004; Mon-Williams et al., 1998; Webster, 2015; Webster et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Observers with typical optical quality show evidence of neural adaptation to their own optical blur.
source: Even observers with typical (i.e., healthy) optical quality show evidence of neural adaptation to their own optical blur, such that modest changes in their own optical aberration pattern severely degrade perceived image quality (Artal et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Distinct neural adaptation mechanisms operate over different timescales.
source: Distinct neural adaptation mechanisms operate over different timescales (Bao and Engel, 2012; Bao et al., 2013; Glasser et al., 2011; Haak et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Most studies have investigated the effects of blur adaptation over short-term periods (i.e., minutes to hours).
source: Most studies have investigated the effects of blur adaptation over short-term periods (i.e., minutes to hours), and often for low magnitudes of blur, thus limiting our understanding of how the adult human brain adapts to large changes in optical quality over longer periods of time (i.e., months to years).
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature, supported by inference from the cited studies.

claim: Adaptive optics can be used to bypass the limits imposed by optical factors while directly assessing visual processing of images free from any optical imperfection.
source: Technological advances in the field of adaptive optics (AO) offer a unique opportunity to bypass the limits imposed by optical factors, while directly assessing visual processing of images free from any optical imperfection (Marcos et al., 2017; Roorda, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on adaptive optics technology.

claim: AO correction in healthy eyes allows observers to detect a larger range of high SF information otherwise indiscernible in the presence of optical blur, improving contrast sensitivity.
source: AO correction in 'healthy' eyes allows observers to detect a larger range of high SF information otherwise indiscernible in the presence of optical blur, improving contrast sensitivity (Liang et al., 1997) and visual acuity (VA) (Yoon and Williams, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Keratoconus is a severe corneal disease afflicting neurotypically-developed adults.
source: KC is a severe corneal disease afflicting neurotypically-developed adults (Vazirani and Basu, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: In keratoconus, the corneal stroma progressively thins and assumes a conical shape, resulting in a substantial increase in both lower-order and higher-order optical aberrations.
source: The corneal stroma progressively thins and assumes a conical shape, resulting in a substantial increase in both lower-order (defocus and astigmatism) and higher-order optical aberrations (HOAs).
evidence: This is a description of the pathophysiology of keratoconus, drawing from established medical knowledge.

claim: Keratoconus is essentially a bilateral condition, although disease development may be highly asymmetric.
source: KC is essentially a bilateral condition, although disease development may be highly asymmetric.
evidence: This is a clinical characteristic of keratoconus, drawing from established medical knowledge.

claim: The onset of keratoconus occurs typically during the late teens or early twenties.
source: The onset of KC occurs typically during the late teens or early twenties, with variable progression that can last until the third or fourth decade of life, when corneal shape generally becomes stable (Vazirani and Basu, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Abnormal corneal conditions such as keratoconus can cause large magnitudes of higher-order aberrations that cannot be efficiently corrected by conventional optical devices.
source: Although HOAs are relatively small in typical eyes, abnormal corneal conditions (e.g., such as KC) can cause large magnitudes of HOAs that cannot be efficiently corrected by conventional optical devices (Maeda et al., 2002; Pantanelli et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Despite their habitual optical correction, keratoconus patients are chronically exposed to severely degraded retinal inputs in their daily life.
source: Thus, despite their habitual optical correction, KC patients are chronically exposed to severely degraded retinal inputs in their daily life.
evidence: This is inferred from the previous statement about HOAs not being correctable by conventional devices.

claim: Neural compensation to image blur improves visual performance in the presence of blur but limits the benefits of improved optical correction.
source: Neural compensation to image blur improves visual performance in the presence of blur but limits the benefits of improved optical correction (e.g., Sabesan and Yoon, 2009; Sabesan and Yoon, 2010; Sawides et al., 2011; Sawides et al., 2010; Vinas et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: When tested under full AO correction, keratoconus patients exhibit considerably poorer visual acuity than that predicted by optical theory or measured in observers with healthy eyes tested under similar AO-corrected optical quality.
source: When tested under full AO correction, KC patients exhibit considerably poorer VA than that predicted by optical theory or measured in observers with healthy eyes tested under similar AO-corrected optical quality (Sabesan and Yoon, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Contrast sensitivity has been a valuable tool for measuring the limits of visual perception for well over a century.
source: For well over a century, contrast sensitivity has been a valuable tool for measuring the limits of visual perception, as well as for the assessment and early diagnosis of many disorders (Campbell and Green, 1965; Fechner, 1860).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to historical research.

claim: The visual system is composed of spatial frequency-selective filters whose combined sensitivity determines the shape of the contrast sensitivity function.
source: The visual system is composed of SF-selective filters whose combined sensitivity determines the shape of the contrast sensitivity function (CSF) (Blakemore and Campbell, 1969; Campbell and Green, 1965; DeValois and DeValois, 1988).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Detection of alterations in the shape of the contrast sensitivity function allows inferences about changes in underlying physiological processes.
source: Detection of alterations in the shape of the CSF allows inferences about changes in underlying physiological processes, such as in amblyopia (Hou et al., 2010), autism spectrum disorder (Guy et al., 2016), and aging (Yan et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on various clinical populations.

claim: Ten keratoconus patients with mild-to-severe optical aberrations and 14 age-matched control observers with healthy eyes were tested monocularly.
source: In total, 10 KC patients with mild-to-severe optical aberrations and 14 age-matched control observers with healthy eyes were tested monocularly (see 'Materials and methods' and Table 1).
evidence: This is a description of the study sample, directly stated in the results.

claim: Habitual optical quality in keratoconus eyes (mean total RMS 3.18 ± 2.09 µm) remained suboptimal compared to control observers (mean total RMS 0.84 ± 0.26 µm) despite their own optical corrections.
source: Relative to the optical quality in age-matched control (CTRL) observers (mean total RMS 0.84 ± 0.26 µm, range 0.58–1.42), habitual optical quality in KC eyes (mean total RMS 3.18 ± 2.09 µm, range 1.36–7.84) remained suboptimal despite their own optical corrections (CTRL-vs-KC total RMS: Mann–Whitney U-test, U = 1, p<0.001, r = 0.99).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study, supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Keratoconus eyes were subject to a substantial amount of uncorrected higher-order aberrations (mean hRMS+ 1.91 ± 1.27 µm), much more than the healthy eyes of control observers (mean hRMS+ 0.37 ± 0.11 µm).
source: Specifically, KC eyes were subject to a substantial amount of uncorrected HOAs (mean hRMS+ 1.91 ± 1.27 µm, range 0.33–4.55), much more than the healthy eyes of control observers (mean hRMS+ 0.37 ± 0.11 µm, range 0.22–0.55) (CTRL-vs-KC hRMS+: Welch's t-test, t = 3.83, p=0.004, d = 1.71).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study, supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Keratoconus eyes were particularly affected by large amounts of vertical coma (mean absolute Z7 coefficient 1.38 ± 0.96 µm), much more than in typical, healthy eyes (0.12 ± 0.11 µm).
source: As previously reported (Pantanelli et al., 2007), KC eyes were particularly affected by large amounts of vertical coma (mean absolute Z7 coefficient 1.38 ± 0.96 µm, range 0.03–2.89), much more than in typical, healthy eyes (0.12 ± 0.11 µm, range 0.02–0.34) (CTRL-vs-KC absolute Z7 coefficient: Welch's t-test, t = 4.11, p=0.003, d = 1.84).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study, supported by statistical analysis and citation to previous research.

claim: The onset of keratoconus in the study patients was around their twenties and varied in its progression.
source: The onset of KC in our patients was around their twenties and varied in its progression, as typically observed in this disease (Vazirani and Basu, 2013).
evidence: This is a description of the study sample, supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The amount of habitual optical aberrations did not correlate with participant's age.
source: As a result, the amount of habitual optical aberrations did not correlate with participant's age (Pearson correlation with habitual RMS r=+0.29, p=0.169; with habitual hRMS+ r=+0.30, p=0.155).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study.

claim: AO correction maintained similar, aberration-free optical quality during visual testing, even in severe keratoconus eyes.
source: Consistent with previous studies from our lab (e.g., Sabesan et al., 2007; Sabesan et al., 2017; Sabesan and Yoon, 2009; Sabesan et al., 2012; Zheleznyak et al., 2016), our AO system allowed us to measure visual performance while effectively maintaining aberration-free optical quality, even in severe KC eyes (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C and citations to previous research.

claim: Aberration-free optical quality under AO correction was similar between control and keratoconus observers.
source: More importantly, aberration-free optical quality under AO correction was similar between CTRL and KC observers (Wilcoxon rank-sum test, U = 50, p=0.259, r = 0.29), with no relation between the individual AO-corrected residual RMS and the amount of habitual optical aberrations without AO correction (Pearson correlation with habitual RMS r=+0.30, p=0.155; with habitual hRMS+ r=+0.33, p=0.120).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study, demonstrating successful AO correction.

claim: Under aberration-free conditions, keratoconus observers exhibited altered contrast sensitivity function relative to control observers, showing impairments for high spatial frequencies (≥ 8.13 cpd) but also improvements for low spatial frequencies (≤ 0.92 cpd).
source: Under similar, aberration-free optical quality, KC observers exhibited altered CSF relative to control observers (Figure 4A), showing impairments for high SFs (for SFs ≥ 8.13 cpd) but also improvements for low SFs (for SFs ≤ 0.92 cpd).
evidence: This is a primary finding from experiment 1, supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The impairment in high-SF cutoff was marginally correlated with the reduction in low-SF truncation across observers (r=+0.38, p=0.0675).
source: Moreover, the impairment in high-SF cutoff was marginally correlated with the reduction in low-SF truncation across observers (r=+0.38, p=0.0675).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from experiment 1.

claim: The area under the contrast sensitivity function was similar between keratoconus and control groups (CTRL 2.63; KC 2.66; p=0.461).
source: Notably, these CSF changes were roughly balanced, resulting in the area under the CSF (AUCSF) being similar between groups (CTRL 2.63 [2.60–2.73]; KC 2.66 [2.60–2.73]; p=0.461).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from experiment 1, supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Both gains and losses in contrast sensitivity under aberration-free conditions were more pronounced in keratoconus patients who experienced large amounts of optical aberrations in their everyday life.
source: Critically, both gains and losses in contrast sensitivity under aberration-free conditions were more pronounced in KC patients who experienced large amounts of optical aberrations in their everyday life (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from experiment 1, supported by data shown in figures.

claim: None of the changes in contrast sensitivity function observed in keratoconus patients correlated with participant's age.
source: Yet, none of the changes in CSF observed in KC patients actually correlated with participant's age (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from experiment 1, shown in a supplementary figure.

claim: Both control and keratoconus groups had better than 20/20 vision when tested under full AO correction.
source: VA measurements using high-contrast Snellen E letters (Figure 5A and 'Materials and methods') showed that both groups had better than 20/20 vision when tested under full AO correction, as expected.
evidence: This is a finding from experiment 2, supported by data.

claim: Keratoconus patients (15.6 ± 1.9 Snellen VA) had poorer visual acuity than control observers (12.6 ± 1.3 Snellen VA) under AO correction.
source: However, KC patients (15.6 ± 1.9 Snellen VA, range 13.4–18.5) had poorer VA than control observers (12.6 ± 1.3 Snellen VA, range 10.6–15.5) (Figure 5B; CTRL-vs-KC logMAR VA: t = 4.68, p<0.001, d = 1.94).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from experiment 2, supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The deficit in high-contrast visual acuity under full AO correction correlated with the participant's amount of habitual aberrations experienced outside the AO.
source: This deficit in high-contrast VA under full AO correction is consistent with previous findings (Sabesan and Yoon, 2009) and correlated with the participant's amount of habitual aberrations experienced outside the AO (Figure 5C; total RMS: r=+0.74, p<0.001; hRMS+: r=+0.79, p<0.001)
evidence: This is a statistical finding from experiment 2, supported by data shown in Figure 5C and citation to previous research.

claim: Visual acuity deficits under AO correction did not correlate with participant's age.
source: but not with participant's age (Figure 5—figure supplement 1; r=+0.24, p=0.250).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from experiment 2, shown in a supplementary figure.

claim: Visual acuity deficits under AO correction correlated with changes in qCSF parameters, including peak SF (r = −0.73, p<0.001), high-SF cutoff (r = −0.74, p<0.001), low-SF truncation (r = −0.66, p<0.001), and low-SF sensitivity (r=+0.42, p=0.039).
source: Moreover, VA deficits under AO correction correlated with the changes in qCSF parameters (Figure 5D), such as peak SF (r = −0.73, p<0.001), high-SF cutoff (r = −0.74, p<0.001), and notably low-SF truncation (r = −0.66, p<0.001) and low-SF sensitivity (r=+0.42, p=0.039).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from experiment 2, shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Poorer visual acuity in keratoconus under AO correction was predicted by both impaired high-SF sensitivity as well as improved low-SF sensitivity.
source: That is, poorer VA in KC under AO correction was predicted by both impaired high-SF sensitivity as well as improved low-SF sensitivity.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the correlation results in experiment 2.

claim: The differences in contrast thresholds between control and keratoconus groups were best explained by a model assuming solely spatial frequency-dependent changes in internal additive noise.
source: Overall, the differences in contrast thresholds between groups were best explained by a simple model assuming solely SF-dependent changes in internal additive noise (Figure 7B; Aadd; r2 = 94.02)
evidence: This is a primary finding from experiment 3, supported by model comparison analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Relative to control observers, severe keratoconus patients showed a reduction in internal additive noise by −49.2% and −53.1% at 0.5 and 1 cpd, respectively.
source: Relative to the control observers, severe KC patients showed a reduction in internal additive noise (Aadd) by −49.2% and −53.1% at 0.5 and 1 cpd, respectively.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the perceptual template model analysis in experiment 3.

claim: At high spatial frequencies, all keratoconus observers exhibited poorer thresholds due to large elevations in internal additive noise.
source: At high SFs, all KC observers exhibited poorer thresholds due to large elevations in internal additive noise, by +21.2% and +110.8% at 9 and 16 cpd for mild/moderate KCs, and by +158.4% and +165% at 9 and 16 cpd for severe KC patients.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the perceptual template model analysis in experiment 3.

claim: Poorer habitual optical quality was associated with reduced individual internal additive noise levels at low spatial frequencies (0.5 and 1 cpd).
source: Consistent with the SF-specific changes in sensitivity observed in KC patients, poorer habitual RMS was associated with reduced individual internal additive noise levels at low SFs (0.5 and 1 cpd) (Figure 8A; total RMS: r = −0.65, p=0.011; hRMS+: r = −0.63, p=0.016).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the hierarchical Bayesian PTM analysis in experiment 3, shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Poorer habitual optical quality was positively correlated with elevated individual internal additive noise levels at high spatial frequencies (9 cpd).
source: We found that poorer habitual optical quality was positively correlated with elevated individual internal additive noise levels at high SFs (Figure 8A; total RMS: r=+0.65, p=0.012; hRMS+: r=+0.70, p=0.005).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the hierarchical Bayesian PTM analysis in experiment 3, shown in Figure 8A.

claim: No correlation was found between habitual optical quality and either multiplicative internal noise or external noise filtering at low or high spatial frequencies.
source: No correlation was found at low or high SFs with either multiplicative internal noise or external noise filtering (Figure 8B, C), supporting the finding that SF-specific changes in internal additive noise alone can account for the impact of long-term exposure to poor optical quality on visual processing.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the hierarchical Bayesian PTM analysis in experiment 3, shown in Figures 8B and 8C.

claim: Long-term exposure to severe optical defects causes a broad functional reallocation of sensory processing resources across a wide range of spatial frequencies, which is mediated by spatial frequency-specific changes in signal enhancement mechanisms.
source: Taken together, the present results reveal that long-term exposure to severe optical defects causes a broad functional reallocation of sensory processing resources across a wide range of SFs, which is mediated by SF-specific changes in signal enhancement mechanisms of SF-selective neurons.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from all three experiments.

claim: The pattern of gains and losses in sensitivity in keratoconus patients reflects spatial frequency-specific changes in signal enhancement mechanisms, with elevated and reduced internal noise levels at high and low spatial frequencies, respectively.
source: The pattern of gains and losses in sensitivity in KC patients reflects SF-specific changes in signal enhancement mechanisms, with elevated and reduced internal noise levels at high and low SFs, respectively.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from experiment 3.

claim: The findings reveal that chronic exposure to poor optical quality does not result in neural deficits restricted to high spatial frequencies, but rather manifests in a functional reallocation of sensory processing resources over a wide range of spatial frequencies.
source: Overall, our findings reveal that chronic exposure to poor optical quality does not result in neural deficits restricted to high SFs, but rather manifests in a functional reallocation of sensory processing resources over a wide range of SFs.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the overall pattern of results.

claim: In typical observers with healthy eyes, the drop in sensitivity at high spatial frequencies is mostly due to blurring from the eye's optics.
source: In typical observers with healthy eyes, the drop in sensitivity at high SFs is mostly due to blurring from the eye's optics (Banks et al., 1987; Campbell and Green, 1965).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Optical blur reduces the strength and reliability of high spatial frequency retinal inputs, leading to weak and unreliable neural responses to fine spatial details.
source: Optical blur reduces the strength and reliability of high-SF retinal inputs, leading to weak and unreliable neural responses to fine spatial details.
evidence: This is an inference based on established knowledge about how optical blur affects visual processing.

claim: The drop in signal-to-noise ratio at high spatial frequencies has been linked to a stronger response to noise with increasing frequency rather than to a change in spatial sensitivity per se.
source: The drop in signal-to-noise ratio at high-SFs has also been linked to a stronger response to noise with increasing frequency rather than to a change in spatial sensitivity per se (Brady and Field, 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: In keratoconus, optical aberrations become approximately six times worse compared to typical levels.
source: In KC, optical aberrations become approximately six times worse compared to typical levels (Pantanelli et al., 2007), strongly attenuating high-SF retinal signals and depriving the visual system from fine spatial information.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Increased internal noise levels of high spatial frequency filters could account for the poorer letter acuity in keratoconus patients when tested under AO correction.
source: Increased internal noise levels of high-SF filters could account for the fact that when tested under AO correction, KC patients showed considerably poorer letter acuity than control observers with typical optical quality whose AO-corrected acuity approaches the limit imposed by photoreceptor sampling.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The improvement in contrast sensitivity at low spatial frequencies in keratoconus was mediated by a reduction in internal additive noise levels of low spatial frequency selective filters.
source: This improvement in contrast sensitivity at low SFs was mediated by a reduction in internal additive noise levels (i.e., improved signal enhancement) of low-SF selective filters, and correlated with the deficits in VA.
evidence: This is a finding from experiment 3, linking the mechanism to the behavioral outcome.

claim: While optical blur strongly degrades high spatial frequency signals, lower spatial frequencies are less compromised by blur and become predominant and more reliable than higher spatial frequencies, especially under large amounts of blur.
source: While optical blur strongly degrades high-SF signals, lower SFs are less compromised by blur and become predominant and more reliable than higher SFs, especially under large amounts of blur.
evidence: This is an inference based on knowledge about how optical blur affects different spatial frequencies.

claim: Keratoconus patients are in a low-pass state of adaptation during natural vision, being deprived of high spatial frequency information and having to rely more on low spatial frequency information to interact with their environment.
source: As a result, KC patients are in a low-pass state of adaptation during natural vision, being deprived of high-SF information and having to rely more on low-SF information to interact with their environment.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the pattern of optical aberrations in keratoconus.

claim: Adaptation acts to maintain sensory systems operating within the limited dynamic range afforded by the brain's limited resources.
source: Adaptation acts to maintain sensory systems operating within the limited dynamic range afforded by the brain's limited resources (Ghodrati et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The contrast sensitivity function reflects an optimal allocation of the brain's limited sensory resources to process a wide range of spatial details.
source: In this context, the CSF reflects an optimal allocation of the brain's limited sensory resources to process a wide range of spatial details.
evidence: This is an inference based on the concept of adaptation and resource allocation.

claim: The pattern of gains and losses in sensitivity observed in keratoconus could reflect neural compensation mechanisms that optimize visual processing to the structure of the degraded retinal inputs.
source: The pattern of gains and losses in sensitivity we observed could reflect neural compensation mechanisms that optimize visual processing to the structure of the degraded retinal inputs.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Short-term adaptation to different stimulus speeds alters the spatiotemporal contrast sensitivity function over a broad range of spatial and temporal frequencies, optimizing visual sensitivity to the new environment.
source: For instance, short-term adaptation to different stimulus speeds alters the spatiotemporal CSF over a broad range of spatial and temporal frequencies, optimizing visual sensitivity to the new environment (Gepshtein et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Cells in the primary visual cortex adaptively change their responses to match the input properties of natural stimulation and enhance information transmission in visual processing.
source: Physiologically, cells in the primary visual cortex (V1) adaptively change their responses to match the input properties of natural (broadband) stimulation and enhance information transmission in visual processing (Sharpee et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Brief adaptation to a single stimulus can reorganize neuronal correlations across an entire network, resulting in specific, stimulus-dependent changes in the population code's efficiency.
source: Moreover, brief adaptation to a single stimulus can reorganize neuronal correlations across an entire network, resulting in specific, stimulus-dependent changes in the population code's efficiency (Gutnisky and Dragoi, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Long-term exposure to severely degraded retinal image quality results in a reallocation of the brain's limited sensory resources, improving visual processing in keratoconus patients across many stimuli and tasks.
source: We conjecture that long-term exposure to severely degraded retinal image quality results in a reallocation of the brain's limited sensory resources, improving visual processing in KC patients across many stimuli and tasks.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Keratoconus participants suffer from poorer acuity under full AO correction, but they actually show substantially better acuity under their own optical quality than typical observers tested under the same degraded optical conditions.
source: Indeed, whereas KC participants suffer from poorer acuity under full AO correction, they actually show substantially better acuity under their own optical quality than typical observers tested under the same degraded optical conditions (Sabesan and Yoon, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Unlike contrast sensitivity, the perceived contrast of gratings above threshold is largely independent of spatial frequency.
source: Unlike contrast sensitivity, the perceived contrast of gratings above threshold is largely independent of SF (Georgeson and Sullivan, 1975).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Contrast constancy is mediated by contrast gain adjustment mechanisms that compensate for earlier attenuation in sensitivity and achieve a 'deblurring' of the retinal image.
source: Contrast constancy is mediated by contrast gain adjustment mechanisms that compensate for earlier attenuation in sensitivity and achieve a 'deblurring' of the retinal image (Georgeson and Sullivan, 1975).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Contrast constancy is tightly linked to the eye's optics.
source: Although we did not directly assess suprathreshold contrast perception, there is evidence that contrast constancy is tightly linked to the eye's optics.
evidence: This is an inference based on cited evidence.

claim: Astigmatic observers show suprathreshold compensation for the orientation-specific neural deficit in contrast sensitivity caused by their uncorrected blur.
source: For instance, astigmatic observers show suprathreshold compensation for the orientation-specific neural deficit in contrast sensitivity caused by their uncorrected blur (Georgeson and Sullivan, 1975).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: All keratoconus patients included in the study reported an onset of the KC-induced optical aberrations around their twenties.
source: All KC patients included in our study reported an onset of the KC-induced optical aberrations around their twenties, which is typical in this disease (Vazirani and Basu, 2013).
evidence: This is a description of the study sample, supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Individual differences in visual processing under AO correction were well accounted for by the amount of habitual optical aberrations experienced by each observer, regardless of participant's age.
source: We found that individual differences in visual processing under AO correction were well accounted for by the amount of habitual optical aberrations experienced by each observer, regardless of participant's age.
evidence: This is a summary of the correlation findings across experiments.

claim: Neural compensation to the eye's optics was primarily driven by the severity of uncorrected optical aberrations rather than by the number of years exposed to uncorrected blur per se.
source: Thus, neural compensation to the eye's optics was primarily driven by the severity of uncorrected optical aberrations rather than by the number of years exposed to uncorrected blur per se.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the lack of correlation with age and the presence of correlation with aberration severity.

claim: All participants included in the study had stable optical quality for at least 1 year before testing.
source: Of note, all the participants included in our study had stable optical quality for at least 1 year before testing.
evidence: This is a description of the study inclusion criteria.

claim: One year of sustained exposure to poor optics is sufficient to cause the neural changes reported in the study.
source: This allows us to conclude that 1 year of sustained exposure to poor optics is sufficient to cause the results reported here.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the study design and inclusion criteria.

claim: Several studies have reported rapid changes in visual processing and early visual cortex activity following short-term periods of sensory deprivation.
source: Several studies have reported rapid changes in visual processing and early visual cortex activity following short-term (i.e., minutes to a few hours) periods of sensory deprivation (Binda et al., 2018; Jamal and Dilks, 2020; Keck et al., 2011; Kwon et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Gradual improvements in vision with time are usually observed during the first months following refractive and cataract surgery, or following correction of relatively low magnitudes of astigmatism.
source: Gradual improvements in vision with time are usually observed during the first months following refractive (Kohnen et al., 2004; Pesudovs, 2005) and cataract (Montés-Micó and Alió, 2003) surgery, or following correction of relatively low magnitudes of astigmatism (Vinas et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Exposure to visual inputs deprived of vertical information over four consecutive days showed limits of neuronal adaptation mechanisms, which peaked during the first day but then dropped in strength despite the adapting environment remaining constant.
source: Moreover, exposure to visual inputs deprived of vertical information over four consecutive days showed limits of neuronal adaptation mechanisms (Haak et al., 2014), which peaked during the first day but then dropped in strength despite the adapting environment remaining constant.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Participants were tested only in one eye.
